units.sourceHTML: Modularity
units.originalInnerHTML: Modularity

units.sourceHTML:
Once you start writing programs that are more than little toys, you quickly run
into two problems:
units.originalInnerHTML:
Once you start writing programs that are more than little toys, you quickly run
into two problems:

units.sourceHTML: You want to break them down into multiple smaller files to make it easier to find your way around them.
units.originalInnerHTML: You want to break them down into multiple smaller files to make it easier to find your way around them.

units.sourceHTML: You want to reuse pieces of them across different programs.
units.originalInnerHTML: You want to reuse pieces of them across different programs.

units.sourceHTML: To address those, Wren has a simple module system. A file containing Wren code defines a module. A module can use the code defined in another module by importing it. You can break big programs into smaller modules that you import, and you can reuse code by having multiple programs share the use of a single module.
units.originalInnerHTML: To address those, Wren has a simple module system. A file containing Wren code defines a module. A module can use the code defined in another module by importing it. You can break big programs into smaller modules that you import, and you can reuse code by having multiple programs share the use of a single module.

units.sourceHTML:
Wren does not have a single global scope. Instead, each module has its own
top-level scope independent of all other modules. This means, for example, that
two modules can define a top-level variable with the same name without causing
a name collision. Each module is, well, modular.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Wren does not have a single global scope. Instead, each module has its own
top-level scope independent of all other modules. This means, for example, that
two modules can define a top-level variable with the same name without causing
a name collision. Each module is, well, modular.

units.sourceHTML: Executing the module #
units.originalInnerHTML: Executing the module #

units.sourceHTML: Once we have the source code for a module, we need to run it. First, the VM takes the fiber that is executing the ⟦CODE0⟧ statement in the importing module and pauses it.
units.originalInnerHTML: Once we have the source code for a module, we need to run it. First, the VM takes the fiber that is executing the import statement in the importing module and pauses it.

units.sourceHTML:
Then it creates a new module object—a new fresh top-level scope,
basically—and a new fiber. It executes the new module’s code in that
fiber and scope. The module can run whatever imperative code it wants and
define whatever top-level variables it wants.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Then it creates a new module object—a new fresh top-level scope,
basically—and a new fiber. It executes the new module’s code in that
fiber and scope. The module can run whatever imperative code it wants and
define whatever top-level variables it wants.

units.sourceHTML:
When the module’s code is done being executed and its fiber completes, the
suspended fiber for the importing module is resumed. This suspending and
resuming is recursive. So, if “a” imports “b” which imports “c”, both “a” and
“b” will be suspended while “c” is running. When “c” is done, “b” is resumed.
Then, when “b” completes, “a” is resumed.
units.originalInnerHTML:
When the module’s code is done being executed and its fiber completes, the
suspended fiber for the importing module is resumed. This suspending and
resuming is recursive. So, if “a” imports “b” which imports “c”, both “a” and
“b” will be suspended while “c” is running. When “c” is done, “b” is resumed.
Then, when “b” completes, “a” is resumed.

units.sourceHTML:
Think of it like traversing the tree of imports, one node at a time. At any
given point in time, only one module’s code is running.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Think of it like traversing the tree of imports, one node at a time. At any
given point in time, only one module’s code is running.

units.sourceHTML: Binding variables #
units.originalInnerHTML: Binding variables #

units.sourceHTML: Once the module is done executing, the last step is to actually import some data from it. Any module can define “top-level” variables. These are simply variables declared outside of any method or function.

units.sourceHTML:
First it runs the “beverages” module. Then it goes through each of the variable
names in the ⟦CODE0⟧ clause. For each one, it looks for a top-level variable with
that name in the imported module. If a variable with that name can’t be found
in the imported module, it’s a runtime error.
units.originalInnerHTML: First it runs the “beverages” module. Then it goes through each of the variable names in the for clause. For each one, it looks for a top-level variable with that name in the imported module. If a variable with that name can’t be found in the imported module, it’s a runtime error.

units.sourceHTML: Otherwise, it gets the current value of the variable and defines a new variable in the importing module with the same name and value. It’s worth noting that the importing module gets its own variable whose value is a snapshot of the value of the imported variable at the time it was imported. If either module later assigns to that variable, the other won’t see it. It’s not a “live” connection.

It’s worth noting that the importing module gets its own variable whose value is a snapshot of the value of the imported variable at the time it was imported. If either module later assigns to that variable, the other won’t see it. It’s not a “live” connection.

In practice, most top-level variables are only assigned once anyway, so this
rarely makes a difference.

units.sourceHTML: Here, “a” and “b” both want to use “shared”. If “shared” defines some top-level state, we only want a single copy of that in memory. To handle this, a module’s code is only executed the first time it is loaded. After that, importing the module again just looks up the previously loaded module.

To handle this, a module’s code is only executed the first time it is loaded. After that, importing the module again just looks up the previously loaded module.

units.sourceHTML:
Internally, Wren maintains a map of every module it has previously loaded. When
a module is imported, Wren looks for it in that map first before it calls out
to the embedder for its source.

a module is imported, Wren looks for it in that map first before it calls out
to the embedder for its source.

You can even have cycles in your imports, provided you’re a bit careful with
them. The loading process, in detail, is:

units.sourceHTML: See if we have already created a module with the given name.

units.sourceHTML: If so, use it.

units.sourceHTML:
Otherwise, create a new module with the name and store it in the module
   registry.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Otherwise, create a new module with the name and store it in the module
   registry.

units.sourceHTML: Create a fiber for it and execute its code.
units.originalInnerHTML: Create a fiber for it and execute its code.

units.sourceHTML: Note the order of the last two steps. When a module is loaded, it is added to the registry before it is executed. This means if an import for that same module is reached while the module itself or one of its imports is executing, it will be found in the registry and the cycle is short-circuited.
